records.value: (a) The curve is U-shaped. As water cooled from 20 °C the capillary column fell, so the volume decreased, until about 4 °C where the volume was at a minimum. Below 4 °C the volume rises again as the water cools toward 0 °C, but this rise is tiny (only about 0.01%), so it may be seen clearly only in pooled class data, the video or the teacher demonstration, and a single group's curve may look flat and noisy near 4 °C. (b) Water has its greatest density at 4 °C, because its volume is smallest there. Most substances keep getting denser and smaller as they cool, so water is anomalous. (c) Volume of ice = mass ÷ density = 500 g ÷ 0.917 g/cm³ = about 545 cm³ (545 ml). Increase = 545 - 500 = about 45 ml. Percentage = 45 ÷ 500 × 100 = about 9%. (d) ΔV = γV₀ΔT describes ordinary expansion where volume increases as temperature rises in a single phase. Here the volume increases as the temperature falls and the water changes state from liquid to a hexagonal ice lattice. This is a phase-change effect that goes beyond the formula. In the sealed bottle, a 9% increase of about 45 ml had nowhere to go, so the pressure on the glass rose until the glass cracked.
